L107@P1: I. BACKGROUND
L108@P1: It is important at the outset for the Court to make clear that this case is not about whether
L109@P1: the challenged Proclamation is good or bad, or the appropriate policy response to the concerns it
L110@P1: describes. These policy questions are the subject of extensive, and often intense, differences of
L111@P1: opinion, and this Court cannot—and does not—express any view as to them. The Court considers
L112@P1: only the legal questions presented here regarding whether the Proclamation and resulting agency
L113@P1: policies exceed the Executive Branch’s constitutional and statutory authority.
L114@P1: The Court also acknowledges that it does not decide this motion—or consider this case—in
L115@P1: a vacuum. Two other lawsuits have challenged the Proclamation and reached different
L116@P1: conclusions. In Chamber of Commerce v. United States Department of Homeland Security, the
L117@P1: district court for the District of Columbia upheld the Proclamation and its $100,000 fee for H-1B
L118@P1: petitions, finding that the President acted within his statutory authority under the Immigration and
L119@P1: Nationality Act (“INA”) and that the agency’s policies implementing the fee did not violate the
L120@P1: Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”). 815 F. Supp. 3d 73, 79 (D.D.C. 2025). The case is
L121@P1: currently on appeal in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit.
L122@P1: In California v. Mullin, the district court for the District of Massachusetts recently declared
L123@P1: unlawful and vacated the Department of Homeland Security’s and the Department of State’s
L124@P1: policies implementing the $100,000 fee. 833 F. Supp. 3d 50, 60–84 (D. Mass. 2026). The First
L125@P1: Circuit later denied the government’s request for a stay pending appeal. See California v. Mullin,
L126@P1: 183 F.4th 42, 46–52 (1st Cir. 2026) (“Mullin II”). The agency policies discussed further below are

L129@P1: judicial review. Cf. Chafin v. Chafin, 568 U.S. 165, 172 (2013) (“As long as the parties have a

L174@P2: A. The H-1B Visa Program
L175@P2: The Immigration and Nationality Act (“INA”) governs the admission of noncitizens into
L176@P2: the United States. See 8 U.S.C. §§ 1101 et seq. To enter the United States, noncitizens must
L177@P2: generally present a valid visa or other travel document, such as a passport, and be found
L178@P2: admissible upon inspection by an immigration officer at a port of entry. See 8 U.S.C. §§ 1181,
L179@P2: 1182(a)(7)(A)(i) and (B)(i), 1185(d), 1201(h), 1225(a); cf. Trump v. Hawaii, 585 U.S. 667, 694
L180@P2: (2018) (recognizing “the basic distinction between admissibility determinations and visa
L181@P2: issuance”).
L182@P2: In 1990 Congress established the H-1B visa program, which provides a pathway for
L183@P2: American employers to hire skilled, nonimmigrant foreign workers in certain “specialty
L184@P2: occupations.”
